title: Toldot: voice and hands (Genesis 27:22)
hook: "The voice is the voice of Jacob, but the hands are the hands of Esau"

segments.voice: Yesterday, wells named Quarrel and Enmity, then Rehoboth. Your line was there's room. This week: a servant's plain prayer, Isaac in the field at evening, two sons at a grave, Rebekah's why, twins in one womb, and room at last. Today, a disguise.

You know someone who says all the right things. Kind words, good values, a great speech at the wedding. Then you watch what they actually do, and it doesn't match. Maybe you've caught yourself doing it too. Genesis has a scene built on exactly that gap. Isaac is old now, his eyes too dim to see, and he wants to give his blessing to his firstborn, Esau. And Rebekah, who heard God say the elder would serve the younger, has a plan.
screen: `THE GREAT SPEECH, THE OTHER DEEDS.` → `ISAAC, OLD AND BLIND.` → `REBEKAH HAS A PLAN.`

segments.voice: Isaac sends Esau out hunting: bring me the food I love, and I'll bless you. Rebekah hears. She cooks two young goats the way Isaac likes them, dresses Jacob in Esau's best clothes, and covers his smooth hands and neck with goatskin, because Esau is hairy. Jacob walks in: I am Esau, your firstborn. Isaac is suspicious. How did you find it so fast? Jacob says God sent it his way. Now he's using God's name in the lie. Come close, Isaac says, let me feel you. He touches the goatskin hands, and then comes the famous line, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "The voice is the voice of Jacob, but the hands are the hands of Esau." Isaac feels the gap: the voice and the hands don't belong to the same person. And still, he gives the blessing. The Torah doesn't hide how uncomfortable this is. Jacob, the quiet one who dwells in tents, lies to his blind father. And the tradition notices that later, Jacob is fooled in the dark himself, by his uncle Laban, when a veiled bride turns out to be the wrong sister. A midrash also turned the line into something else: when Jacob's voice is heard in prayer and study, the hands of Esau have no power. Both readings live side by side. One says a voice matters. The other asks: does your voice match your hands? Jewish ethics has a phrase for that: that your inside be like your outside. What you say and what you do, from the same person.
screen: `GOATSKIN ON SMOOTH HANDS.` · `I AM ESAU, YOUR FIRSTBORN.` · `ISAAC FEELS THE GAP.` · `INSIDE LIKE OUTSIDE.` · then, large: `THE VOICE IS THE VOICE OF JACOB.`

segments.voice: Think of one thing you say about yourself: I'm a good friend, I care about my health, family comes first. Now look at what your hands actually did this week, where voice and hands line up, and where there's a gap. Don't beat yourself up; just choose one small place to close it.
Toldot. Generations: the portion where Jacob, in goatskin, fools his blind father, who feels a voice and hands that don't match.
Your line: voice and hands the same. Inside like outside. Day one hundred eighty-nine, done.

howItsDone: Jewish ethics speaks of tokho k'varo, that a person's inside be like their outside, and the story of Jacob's disguise is studied each year with open discussion of what he did.

fork.setup: you're Isaac. the voice sounds like Jacob. the hands feel like Esau. what do you do?
fork.reveal: Isaac said, the voice is the voice of Jacob, but the hands are the hands of Esau, and blessed him anyway.

trapdoor: what you thought: a clever trick with goatskins.
what it means: a blind father feels the gap between a voice and a pair of hands.
what a scholar hears: Genesis Rabbah 65:20 turns the line into a teaching about the power of Jacob's voice in prayer and study.

disguises, the goatskin on Jacob's hands

notes: Genesis Rabbah 65:20 (the voice of Jacob in synagogues and study houses; Esau's hands powerless) cited from memory; confirm.
The connection between Jacob's deception and Laban's (measure for measure) is drawn in midrash (e.g. Genesis Rabbah 70:19); stated generally. Confirm.
'Tokho k'varo' (inside like outside) from Yoma 72b; confirm.
Jacob invoking God in the lie (27:20) is stated plainly; a Keeper may want gentler framing.
